title: Famous Rock Gardens Around the World
text:
Some of the finest rock gardens on the planet serve both as horticultural collections and as inspiration for gardeners of every level. Visiting — or even just studying — these great gardens can transform your understanding of what is possible with stone and plants.


The rock garden at the Royal Horticultural Society’s garden at Wisley, Surrey is one of the largest and most celebrated in Britain. Originally constructed in 1911, it covers several acres of a natural hillside and features thousands of alpine and rock plants arranged in a series of beds, slopes, and water features.
The garden is particularly renowned for its spring display, when gentians, primulas, saxifrages, and phlox create vivid sweeps of colour across the rock faces. It is maintained by a dedicated team of alpine specialists and is regularly updated with new plant introductions.






Tip



Visitor tip: The Wisley rock garden is at its peak in April and May. If you can visit only once, aim for this window.





The Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew houses one of the world’s great plant collections, and its alpine section is no exception. Kew’s Davies Alpine House — a striking glasshouse opened in 2006 — provides a controlled environment for growing some of the most challenging high-altitude plants from around the world.
The structure is designed to keep plants cool and well-ventilated in summer while protecting them from excessive British rainfall in winter — conditions that mirror the snowpack environment of a high mountain.



The Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh maintains one of Scotland’s finest rock gardens, built in 1908 from Perthshire sandstone. Its collection includes plants from alpine habitats across Asia, the Americas, and Europe, with a particular strength in Himalayan species.
Edinburgh’s cooler, wetter climate is actually an asset for many high-altitude plants that struggle in the warmer south of England, and the garden benefits from a naturally dramatic topography.



While best known for its sweeping Palladian landscape, Stourhead (National Trust) also features a historic grotto and rocky cascade that incorporates planting in the rock garden tradition. It demonstrates how stone and water can be combined with planting to create deeply atmospheric garden spaces.



Nestled within the Jardin des Plantes in Paris, the Jardin Alpin is a remarkable collection of mountain plants from across the globe, arranged within a rocky landscape. Established in the early 20th century, it contains over 2,000 species representing alpine flora from the Pyrenees, Alps, Himalayas, and beyond.
The garden is a testament to French botanical tradition and remains an important living collection for research and education.



The Gothenburg Botanical Garden in Sweden is home to one of northern Europe’s most impressive rock gardens. Its naturalistic design incorporates large granite outcrops — typical of the Scandinavian landscape — and features an exceptional collection of Scandinavian, North American, and Asian alpines.
The garden is particularly noted for its crevice planting, with plants established in narrow gaps between rock faces — a technique that is the focus of Module 6 in this course.



Studying these gardens reveals several principles that apply at every scale:

Rock placement matters — the finest rock gardens use stone that appears to emerge naturally from the ground, with strata lines running consistently
Scale is relative — a well-planted stone trough can be as visually compelling as an acre of alpine beds
Plant knowledge is everything — the greatest rock gardeners are first and foremost great botanists
Time is the final ingredient — all of these gardens have matured over decades, with plants slowly colonising every available niche







Note



Activity: Choose one of the gardens above and explore it further — most have detailed websites, plant databases, and virtual tours. Make a note of three plants you see that you would like to grow, and keep them in mind as you work through the rest of this course.





From Surrey to Stockholm, the world’s great rock gardens share a common language: carefully placed stone, sharply drained planting, and plants chosen for their ability to thrive in challenging conditions. They are monuments to patience, botanical knowledge, and a deep respect for the natural world.
In the modules that follow, you will develop the skills to bring these same principles to your own garden — whatever its size.

title: Welcome
text:
Welcome to one of horticulture’s most captivating disciplines — rock gardening. This course will guide you through the art and science of cultivating flowering plants in, on, and around rocky landscapes.
Whether you have a small courtyard, a sloping hillside, or simply a stone trough on a balcony, rock gardening offers a way to work with nature rather than against it. Many of the most spectacular flowering plants in the world have evolved to thrive in harsh, rocky environments — and with the right knowledge, you can recreate that magic at home.


Over nine modules, this course covers everything you need to go from bare stone to blooming beauty:

The history and traditions of rock gardening, from Victorian alpine houses to contemporary naturalistic design
How lithophytic plants — those that grow on or in rock — survive and thrive without conventional soil
How to choose and position rocks to suit both plants and aesthetics
Soil mixes, drainage, and planting techniques for crevice gardens, scree beds, and troughs
Plant selection by season, colour, and companion grouping
Maintenance, troubleshooting, and propagation to keep your garden thriving year-round
Inspiring projects you can try yourself, from tabletop troughs to hillside transformations




Modules are designed to be worked through in order, as each builds on the last. However, if you are already experienced in one area — say, plant propagation — feel free to skip ahead to the topics most relevant to you.






Tip



Tip: Keep a gardening notebook as you work through the course. Sketching ideas, jotting down plant names, and recording what works in your garden are the habits of every great rock gardener.





Rock gardens are not instant creations. The finest examples have been tended for decades, with plants slowly maturing and self-seeding into every crack and crevice. Part of the joy is watching a garden evolve over years — each season bringing new discoveries.
Let’s begin. Module 1 starts with the big question: What exactly is rock gardening?

title: What is Rock Gardening?
text:
Rock gardening is the practice of cultivating plants — particularly flowering alpines and other hardy species — in a setting that mimics rocky, mountainous, or stony natural habitats. At its heart, it is an exercise in imitation: recreating the conditions that allow some of the world’s most beautiful and resilient plants to thrive.


The modern rock garden has its roots in 19th-century Britain, when botanists and explorers began returning from the Alps, the Himalayas, and other mountain ranges with extraordinary plants that defied conventional cultivation. Early attempts to grow these alpines in flat, humus-rich borders largely failed — the plants rotted, suffocated, or simply refused to perform.
The solution, pioneered by plantsmen such as Reginald Farrer (1880–1920), was to recreate the plants’ native conditions: sharply drained, gritty soil; exposed, sunny aspects; and the temperature-buffering effect of surrounding rock. Farrer’s influential book The English Rock Garden (1919) set the template for rock garden design that still resonates today.
By the early 20th century, rock gardens had become a fashionable feature of grand estates and public parks across Britain and Europe. The Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew, Edinburgh, and Wisley all developed significant rock garden collections during this period.



A rock garden is defined less by its size and more by its principles:

Rocky structure — stones are placed to create crevices, ledges, and pockets where plants can root
Sharp drainage — water moves through the growing medium quickly, preventing root rot
Appropriate plants — species selected for their ability to thrive in exposed, nutrient-poor, well-drained conditions
Naturalistic design — rocks arranged to suggest a natural outcrop rather than a formal arrangement

Rock gardens can range from a small stone trough on a windowsill planted with miniature sedums, to a vast alpine meadow covering an entire hillside.










Type
Description




Alpine garden
Mimics high-altitude mountain habitats; often features a scree or moraine bed


Scree garden
A deep bed of fine gravel and grit, replicating the loose stone slopes below mountain cliffs


Trough garden
Plants grown in a stone or hypertufa trough; ideal for small spaces and miniature varieties


Crevice garden
Rocks placed vertically or at angles to create narrow planting pockets


Dry stone wall
A freestanding or retaining wall whose gaps are planted with trailing and cushion-forming species


Peat bed
A variation using acidic conditions to suit ericaceous and woodland-edge plants






Beyond the historical tradition, rock gardening offers a number of compelling benefits:

Year-round interest — with careful plant selection, something is always in flower from late winter to autumn
Low maintenance — once established, many alpine and rock plants are highly self-sufficient
Wildlife value — open, sunny rock gardens attract bees, butterflies, and other pollinators
Space efficiency — some of the most spectacular rock plants are tiny; a single trough can hold dozens of species
Sustainability — well-designed rock gardens require little watering, no mowing, and minimal intervention







Note



Did you know? Some of the world’s most beloved flowering plants — including gentians, saxifrages, and lewisias — are naturally lithophytic, meaning they evolved to grow on or among rocks with little or no conventional soil.





Successful rock gardening requires a shift in thinking. Where conventional gardeners seek rich, moisture-retentive soil, the rock gardener seeks the opposite: lean, gritty, and fast-draining. Where the conventional border thrives in sheltered shade, the rock garden mostly demands sun and exposure.
Learning to think like an alpine plant — understanding what it evolved for and what conditions it needs to thrive — is the foundation of everything that follows in this course.






Tip



Reflection: Think about a rocky landscape you have visited — a hillside, a sea cliff, a stone wall — and recall what was growing there. Chances are those plants were tougher, more compact, and more colourful than you might expect. That resilience is exactly what we are harnessing.
